attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own newsletter post.

semantics.note: 'Will eventually come' is a firm forecast with no deadline. 'Maybe in the next decade' is hedged, and the proposition correctly keeps it as only a possibility.

contract.note: Reading AGI as broadly accepted, independently tested general competence is fair and ordinary. The contract rightly treats the decade as no deadline, though its 2035 horizon interval sits awkwardly with that. Only proof of impossibility could contradict the claim.

evidence.note: Dated on the evaluation date. It calls the claim that AGI has arrived inconclusive, so it shows neither broadly accepted AGI nor impossibility.

reviews.rationale: This is a firm forecast of eventual AGI with no deadline. The packet shows no independently confirmed, broadly accepted AGI: the GPT-6 Astra claims are disputed, and e1 calls the evidence inconclusive. Nothing shows AGI is impossible. Neither the support nor the contradiction condition is met, so the claim stays unresolved.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own newsletter post.

semantics.note: 'Safe to say ... won't' signals high confidence, not a hedge, so this is a scored forecast. In context, 'lead the way' points toward AGI and new approaches. GPT-5 and METR are reasons he gives, not conditions.

contract.note: Reading 'lead the way' as supplying the main approach behind the first accepted AGI is a fair contextual reading. Treating hybrid systems built on LLMs as still LLM-based is reasonable, but the speaker never supplied that rule.

evidence.note: OpenAI's own announcement of GPT-6 Astra with benchmark claims. It establishes neither broadly accepted AGI nor what mainly drives the model's capability.

reviews.rationale: There is no deadline. No independently confirmed, broadly accepted AGI exists in the packet. The GPT-6 Astra evidence is a company disclosure and settles neither whether AGI arrived nor what approach drove it. Without a qualifying AGI and evidence about its architecture, the forecast cannot be scored.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words. He characterises the METR study's finding and endorses it.

semantics.note: The proposition drops the 'a METR study shows' framing and reads more generally than the statement. The contract restores the study scope, which keeps the claim faithful overall.

contract.note: Limiting the claim to the cited study's setting and period (Feb–Jun 2025) is a fair, ordinary reading of what the referenced study shows. It neither stretches the claim into a universal one nor shrinks it.

evidence.note: METR's own summary: AI slowed experienced developers by 19% despite impressive benchmark scores. METR explicitly draws this contrast.
The paper's caveats warn against generalising beyond the study. The paper also says the slowdown suggests real-world capability may be lower than benchmarks imply.
A later follow-up with newer tools and a different period. It has selection problems and does not overturn the 2025 result.

reviews.rationale: The cited METR study found a 19% slowdown in real practice and itself contrasts this with impressive benchmark results. That matches Marcus's description of the study. The caveats and the later follow-up limit how far the result generalises, but they do not reject the study-specific claim.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own newsletter post.

semantics.note: The 'whale' is AGI in context. The proposition captures both parts: nobody had delivered AGI, and Grok-4 and Llama-4 underwhelmed.

contract.note: Reading 'underwhelmed' as falling short of launch hype or the makers' claims is fair and ordinary. It does not require the models to be bad in absolute terms.

evidence.note: Altman conceded GPT-5 does not meet his own AGI definition. That supports 'nobody delivered' for the leading lab.
Contemporaneous report: Llama 4's headline score came from an unreleased variant, and Meta had to defend the launch.
Meta delayed Llama 4 Behemoth over quality concerns, after its in-house AI work ran into problems.
A contemporaneous review found Grok 4 apparently overtrained on benchmarks and not useful enough for everyday tasks.
Some users valued Grok 4 for planning and hard bugs. This is weak counterevidence showing mixed, not uniformly poor, reception.

reviews.rationale: No lab had delivered accepted AGI by August 2025, and OpenAI's CEO conceded GPT-5 was not AGI. Llama 4 had a benchmark controversy and its flagship model was delayed. Grok 4's real-world reception lagged its benchmark-driven launch. Some positive Grok 4 feedback falls well short of the contradiction condition (being broadly received as meeting the hype).
